replacement: [Enter the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely.]
[Exeunt.]
[Enter King Henry, Gloucester, Bedford, Clarence, Warwick, Westmorland, Exeter and Attendants.]
KING HENRY V. Where is my gracious Lord of Canterbury?
KING HENRY V. Send for him, good uncle.
KING HENRY V. Not yet, my cousin. Before we hear him, we want some weighty matters settled. They are weighing on our mind, and they concern us and France.
[Enter the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely.]

KING HENRY V. We thank you, truly. My learned lord, we ask you to go on and explain, justly and with a clear religious conscience, whether the Salic law they have in France does or does not bar our claim. And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord, that you should twist, strain or bend your reading of it. God forbid that you should burden your conscience by laying out claims that are falsely made, whose right does not fit the truth in its natural colors. For God knows how many men now in good health will shed their blood to prove whatever your reverence urges us to. So take care how you pledge our person, and how you wake our sleeping sword of war. We charge you in God's name, take care. Two such kingdoms have never fought without much bloodshed. Every innocent drop of it is a grief and a bitter complaint against the man whose wrongs sharpen the swords that cause such waste of short human lives. Under this solemn charge, speak, my lord. We will listen, take note, and believe in our heart that what you say has been washed in your conscience as pure as a sin washed away by baptism.
KING HENRY V. Can I make this claim with right and a clear conscience?
KING HENRY V. We must not only arm to invade the French. We must also set aside forces to defend against the Scot, who will raid us at every advantage.

KING HENRY V. We don't only mean the roving snatchers. We fear the Scot's main design, for he has always been a fickle neighbor to us. You will read that my great-grandfather never went into France with his forces without the Scot pouring down on his unguarded kingdom like the tide through a breach, with the whole brimming fullness of his strength. He galled the stripped land with fierce attacks and ringed castles and towns with a grim siege. England, empty of defense, shook and trembled at such a bad neighbor.
KING HENRY V. Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.
[Exeunt some Attendants.]
[Enter Ambassadors of France.]

KING HENRY V. We are no tyrant but a Christian king. Our anger is as much under the control of our mercy as the wretches chained in our prisons. So tell us the Dauphin's mind with frank and unrestrained plainness.
KING HENRY V. What treasure, uncle?

KING HENRY V. We are glad the Dauphin is so playful with us. We thank you for his gift and for your trouble. When we have matched our rackets to these balls, we will play a set in France, by God's grace, that will knock his father's crown into the hazard. Tell him he has made a match with such a quarrelsome player that all the courts of France will be disturbed with chases. And we understand him well, the way he throws our wilder days in our face without weighing what use we made of them. We never valued this poor seat of England. So, living away from it, we gave ourselves over to wild license, as it is common that men are merriest when they are away from home. But tell the Dauphin I will keep my royal state, act like a king, and spread the sail of my greatness when I rouse myself on my throne of France. Because I have put aside my majesty and plodded like a working man on working days. But I will rise there in such full glory that I will dazzle every eye in France, and strike the Dauphin blind to look at us. And tell the playful prince that this mock of his has turned his balls into cannonballs. His soul will be heavily charged for the wasteful vengeance that will fly with them. For this mock of his will mock many thousands of widows out of their dear husbands, mock mothers out of their sons, and mock castles down. And some who are not yet conceived or born will have cause to curse the Dauphin's scorn. But all this lies in the will of God, to whom I appeal, and in whose name you can tell the Dauphin I am coming on, to avenge myself as I can and to put forth my rightful hand in a well-blessed cause. So go in peace, and tell the Dauphin his jest will taste only of shallow wit, when thousands weep more than ever laughed at it. — Escort them with safe conduct. — Farewell.
[Exeunt Ambassadors.]

KING HENRY V. We hope to make the sender blush at it. So, my lords, let no good hour pass that can help our expedition. We have no thought in us now but France, except for those we owe to God, which come before our business. So let our forces for this war be gathered soon, and let everything be thought of that can add more feathers to our wings with reasonable speed. For, God before us, we'll scold this Dauphin at his father's door. So let every man now put his mind to work, so that this fair undertaking can be set in motion.
[Exeunt.]
[Flourish. Enter Chorus.]
[Exit.]
[Enter Corporal Nym and Lieutenant Bardolph.]
[Enter Pistol and Hostess.]

HOSTESS. No, by my word, not for long. We can't lodge and feed a dozen or fourteen gentlewomen who make an honest living with the prick of their needles without people at once thinking we run a brothel. [_Nym and Pistol draw._] Oh, alas, Our Lady, if he isn't drawing his sword now! We'll see deliberate adultery and murder committed.
[Draws.]
[Enter the Boy.]
[Exeunt Hostess and Boy.]
[They draw.]
[Enter Hostess.]
PISTOL. Nym, you've spoken right. His heart is broken and strengthened.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Exeter, Bedford and Westmorland.]
[Trumpets sound. Enter King Henry, Scroop, Cambridge and Grey.]

KING HENRY V. Now the wind is fair, and we will go aboard. My Lord of Cambridge, my kind Lord of Masham, and you, my gentle knight, give me your thoughts. Don't you think the forces we bring with us will cut their way through the power of France, and carry out the task for which we have gathered them?

KING HENRY V. I don't doubt that, since we are sure that we take with us no heart that doesn't grow in fair agreement with ours. And we leave behind none that doesn't wish success and conquest to attend us.
KING HENRY V. Then we have great cause to be thankful. And we will forget how to use our hand sooner than we will forget to repay deserving service, according to its weight and worth.

KING HENRY V. We expect no less. Uncle Exeter, set free the man who was jailed yesterday for railing against our person. We consider that it was too much wine that set him on, and on second thought we pardon him.
KING HENRY V. Oh, let us still be merciful.

KING HENRY V. Alas, your too great love and care for me weigh heavily as prayers against this poor wretch! If little faults that come from drink are not to be winked at, how shall we open our eyes when capital crimes, chewed, swallowed and digested, appear before us? We will set that man free anyway, though Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, in their dear care and tender protection of our person, would have him punished. And now to our French business. Who are the recent commissioners?

KING HENRY V. Then, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, there is yours. There is yours, Lord Scroop of Masham. And, sir knight, Grey of Northumberland, this one is yours. Read them, and know that I know your worth. My Lord of Westmorland, and uncle Exeter, we will go aboard tonight. — Why, what is this, gentlemen! What do you see in those papers that makes you lose so much color? — Look how they change! Their cheeks are paper. — Why, what do you read there, that has so cowed your blood and chased it out of sight?

KING HENRY V. The mercy that was alive in us only a moment ago has been suppressed and killed by your own advice. For shame, you must not dare to talk of mercy, because your own arguments turn back on you, as dogs turn on their masters, and tear at you. See, my princes and my noble peers, these English monsters! My Lord of Cambridge here, you know how readily our love agreed to supply him with everything that belonged to his honor. And this man, for a few light crowns, lightly conspired and swore himself to the schemes of France to kill us here at Southampton. This knight, bound to us by our generosity no less than Cambridge is, has sworn the same. But oh, what shall I say to you, Lord Scroop? You cruel, ungrateful, savage and inhuman creature! You who carried the key to all my counsels, who knew the very bottom of my soul, who could almost have coined me into gold if you had wanted to use me for your own profit. Is it possible that foreign pay could draw out of you one spark of evil that might hurt my finger? It is so strange that, though the truth of it stands out as plain as black and white, my eye can scarcely see it. Treason and murder always kept together, like two devils yoked and sworn to each other's purpose. They worked so openly, for such natural causes, that no one cried out in wonder at them. But you, against all proportion, brought wonder in to wait on treason and murder. And whatever cunning fiend it was that worked on you so perversely has won the prize in hell for excellence. Other devils who tempt men to treason botch and bungle up damnation with patches, colors and forms borrowed from glittering shows of piety. But he who shaped you told you to stand up. He gave you no reason to commit treason, except to dub you with the name of traitor. If that same demon who has fooled you so were to walk the whole world with his lion's stride, he could go back to vast Tartarus and tell the legions, "I can never win a soul so easily as that Englishman's." Oh, how you have infected the sweetness of trust with suspicion! Do men seem dutiful? Why, so did you. Do they seem serious and learned? Why, so did you. Do they come from noble families? Why, so did you. Do they seem religious? Why, so did you. Or are they sparing in diet, free from crude passion, whether of mirth or anger, steady in spirit, not swerving with their blood, dressed and adorned in modest manners, not trusting the eye without the ear, and trusting neither except after purified judgment? You seemed such, and so finely sifted. And so your fall has left a kind of blot that casts some suspicion on the fullest and best-endowed man. I will weep for you. For this revolt of yours, I think, is like a second fall of man. Their faults are plain. Arrest them to answer to the law. And may God acquit them of their plots!

KING HENRY V. May God acquit you in his mercy! Hear your sentence. You conspired against our royal person. You joined with an openly declared enemy and received from his coffers the golden down payment for our death. In this you would have sold your king to slaughter, his princes and peers to slavery, his subjects to oppression and contempt, and his whole kingdom to ruin. As for our own person, we seek no revenge. But we must so cherish the safety of our kingdom, whose ruin you sought, that we hand you over to her laws. So go from here, poor miserable wretches, to your death. May God in his mercy give you patience to endure the taste of it, and true repentance for all your grievous offenses! Take them away.
[Exeunt Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, guarded.]
[Flourish. Exeunt.]
[Enter Pistol, Nym, Bardolph, Boy and Hostess.]
BOY. Yes, he did. He said they were devils incarnate.
[Kissing her.]
[Exeunt.]
[Flourish. Enter the French King, the Dauphin, the Dukes of Berry and Brittany, the Constable and others.]
[Enter a Messenger.]
[Exeunt Messenger and certain Lords.]
[Enter Exeter.]
[Flourish.]
[Exeunt.]
[Flourish. Enter Chorus.]
[Alarum, and chambers go off.]
[Exit.]
[Alarum. Enter King Henry, Exeter, Bedford, Gloucester and Soldiers, with scaling-ladders.]

KING HENRY V. Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more, or close the wall up with our English dead! In peace there's nothing so becomes a man as quiet stillness and humility. But when the blast of war blows in our ears, then imitate the tiger. Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood, disguise fair nature with hard-faced rage. Then give your eyes a terrible look. Let them peer out through the opening of your head like brass cannon. Let your brow hang over them as fearfully as a battered rock overhangs and juts above its worn base, swilled by the wild and wasteful ocean. Now clench your teeth and flare your nostrils wide, hold your breath hard, and bend every spirit up to its full height. On, on, you noblest English, whose blood comes from fathers proven in war! Those fathers, like so many Alexanders, fought in these parts from morning to evening, and sheathed their swords only when they ran out of enemies. Do not dishonor your mothers. Now prove that the men you called fathers really did beget you. Be a pattern now to men of coarser blood, and teach them how to fight. And you, good yeomen, whose limbs were made in England, show us here the mettle of your pasture. Let us swear that you are worth your breeding, which I do not doubt. For there is none of you so low and base that he has no noble gleam in his eyes. I see you standing like greyhounds in the leash, straining to start. The game's afoot! Follow your spirit, and on this charge cry, "God for Harry! England and Saint George!"
[Exeunt. Alarum, and chambers go off.]
[Enter Nym, Bardolph, Pistol and Boy.]
BOY. As regularly, but not as truly, as a bird sings on a bough.
[Enter Fluellen.]
[Driving them forward.]
[Exeunt all but Boy.]
[Exit.]
[Enter Gower and Fluellen.]
[Enter Macmorris and Captain Jamy.]
[A parley sounded.]
[Exeunt.]
[The Governor and some citizens on the walls; the English forces below. Enter King Henry and his train.]

KING HENRY V. How does the governor of the town resolve? This is the last parley we will allow. So give yourselves up to our best mercy, or defy us to do our worst, like men proud of their own destruction. For as I am a soldier, which is the name that suits me best in my thoughts, if I begin the bombardment again, I will not leave half-conquered Harfleur until it lies buried in its ashes. The gates of mercy will all be shut. The bloodied soldier, rough and hard of heart, will range free with a bloody hand and a conscience wide as hell, mowing down like grass your fresh young virgins and your blossoming infants. What is that to me, if wicked War, dressed in flames like the prince of fiends, does with his sooty face all the cruel deeds that go with waste and desolation? What is it to me, when you yourselves are the cause, if your pure maidens fall into the hands of hot and forceful rape? What rein can hold licentious wickedness when it runs its fierce course down the hill? We might as uselessly spend our empty commands on enraged soldiers in their plunder as send orders to the leviathan to come ashore. So, you men of Harfleur, take pity on your town and your people, while my soldiers are still under my command, while the cool and gentle wind of grace still blows away the filthy and infectious clouds of reckless murder, plunder and villainy. If not, why, in a moment expect to see the blind and bloody soldier defile with foul hand the hair of your shrill-shrieking daughters. Your fathers will be seized by their silver beards, and their most reverend heads dashed against the walls. Your naked infants will be spitted on pikes, while their mad mothers, with confused howls, split the clouds, as the wives of Jewry did at Herod's bloody-minded slaughtermen. What do you say? Will you yield and avoid this, or be guilty in your defense and be destroyed like this?

KING HENRY V. Open your gates. Come, uncle Exeter, go and enter Harfleur. Stay there and fortify it strongly against the French. Show mercy to them all. As for us, dear uncle, with winter coming on and sickness growing among our soldiers, we will retire to Calais. Tonight we will be your guests in Harfleur. Tomorrow we are ready to march.
[Flourish. The King and his train enter the town.]
[Enter Katherine and Alice, an old Gentlewoman.]
KATHERINE. _Alice, tu as été en Angleterre, et tu parles bien le langage._ — Alice, you have been in England, and you speak the language well. —
KATHERINE. _Je te prie, m'enseignez; il faut que j'apprenne à parler. Comment appelez-vous la main en anglais?_ — Please teach me; I must learn to speak it. What do you call the hand in English? —
KATHERINE. De hand. _Et les doigts?_ — And the fingers? —

KATHERINE. _La main_ — the hand — de hand; _les doigts_ — the fingers — de fingres. _Je pense que je suis le bon écolier; j'ai gagné deux mots d'anglais vitement. Comment appelez-vous les ongles?_ — I think I am a good pupil; I have won two English words quickly. What do you call the nails? —
KATHERINE. De nails. _Écoutez; dites-moi, si je parle bien:_ — Listen; tell me if I speak well: — de hand, de fingres, _et_ — and — de nails.
KATHERINE. _Dites-moi l'anglais pour le bras._ — Tell me the English for the arm. —
KATHERINE. _Et le coude?_ — And the elbow? —
KATHERINE. D'elbow. _Je m'en fais la répétition de tous les mots que vous m'avez appris dès à présent._ — I will repeat all the words you have taught me so far. —
KATHERINE. _Excusez-moi, Alice. Écoutez:_ — Excuse me, Alice. Listen: — d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, de bilbow.
KATHERINE. _O Seigneur Dieu, je m'en oublie!_ D'elbow. _Comment appelez-vous le col?_ — Oh Lord God, I forget it! — D'elbow. — What do you call the neck? —
KATHERINE. De nick. _Et le menton?_ — And the chin? —
KATHERINE. De sin. _Le col_ — the neck — de nick; _le menton_ — the chin — de sin.
KATHERINE. _Je ne doute point d'apprendre, par la grâce de Dieu, et en peu de temps._ — I do not doubt that I will learn, by the grace of God, and in a short time. —
KATHERINE. _Non, je réciterai à vous promptement:_ — No, I will recite to you promptly: — d'hand, de fingres, de mails,—
KATHERINE. De nails, de arm, de ilbow.
KATHERINE. _Ainsi dis-je_ — So I say — d'elbow, de nick, _et_ — and — de sin. _Comment appelez-vous le pied et la robe?_ — What do you call the foot and the gown? —

KATHERINE. De foot _et_ — and — de coun! _O Seigneur Dieu! ils sont les mots de son mauvais, corruptible, gros, et impudique, et non pour les dames d'honneur d'user. Je ne voudrais prononcer ces mots devant les seigneurs de France pour tout le monde. Foh!_ — Oh Lord God! They are words of a bad sound, corrupt, gross and shameless, and not for ladies of honor to use. I would not pronounce those words before the lords of France for anything in the world. Foh! — le foot _et_ le coun! _Néanmoins, je réciterai une autre fois ma leçon ensemble:_ — Nevertheless, I will recite my whole lesson once more together: — d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, d'elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, de coun.
KATHERINE. _C'est assez pour une fois. Allons-nous à dîner._ — That is enough for one time. Let us go to dinner. —
[Exeunt.]
[Enter the King of France, the Dauphin, the Duke of Bourbon, the Constable of France and others.]
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Gower and Fluellen, meeting.]
[Enter Pistol.]
[Exit.]
[Drum and colors. Enter King Henry, Gloucester and his poor soldiers.]
KING HENRY V. How now, Fluellen! Did you come from the bridge?
KING HENRY V. What men have you lost, Fluellen?

KING HENRY V. We would have all such offenders cut off like that. And we give strict orders that in our marches through the country nothing is to be forced from the villages, nothing taken that is not paid for, and none of the French is to be insulted or abused in scornful language. For when gentleness and cruelty play for a kingdom, the gentler player is the sooner winner.
[Tucket. Enter Montjoy.]
KING HENRY V. Well then, I know you. What shall I learn from you?
KING HENRY V. Unfold it.
KING HENRY V. What is your name? I know your rank.

KING HENRY V. You do your office fairly. Turn back and tell your King I do not seek him now. But I would be willing to march on to Calais without interference. To tell the truth, though it is no wisdom to confess so much to an enemy of craft and advantage, my people are much weakened by sickness, my numbers are reduced, and the few I have are almost no better than that many Frenchmen. Yet when they were healthy, I tell you, herald, I thought one pair of English legs could march three Frenchmen. Still, forgive me, God, that I brag like this! This air of France has blown that vice into me. I must repent. So go and tell your master I am here. My ransom is this frail and worthless body, and my army only a weak and sickly guard. Yet, with God before us, tell him we will come on, though France himself and another neighbor like him stand in our way. Here is something for your trouble, Montjoy. Go and tell your master to think carefully. If we may pass, we will. If we are hindered, we shall discolor your tawny ground with your red blood. And so, Montjoy, farewell. The sum of all our answer is only this. We would not seek a battle as we are. Nor, as we are, will we say we will avoid it. So tell your master.
[Exit.]
KING HENRY V. We are in God's hands, brother, not in theirs. March to the bridge. It is getting toward night. Beyond the river we'll make camp, and tomorrow tell them to march away.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter the Constable of France, the Lord Rambures, Orleans, Dauphin with others.]
[Exit.]
[Enter a Messenger.]
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Chorus.]
[Exit.]
[Enter King Henry, Bedford and Gloucester.]

KING HENRY V. Gloucester, it's true that we are in great danger. So our courage should be all the greater. Good morning, brother Bedford. God Almighty! There is some soul of goodness in evil things, if men would watch for it and distil it out. Our bad neighbour makes us early risers, which is both healthy and good management. Besides, our enemies are our outward consciences. They are preachers to us all, warning us to dress ourselves well for our end. So we can gather honey from the weed and draw a moral lesson from the devil himself.
[Enter Erpingham.]

KING HENRY V. It's good for men to learn to love their present pains from example. That eases the spirit. And when the mind is quickened, no doubt, the body's organs, though dead and lifeless before, break out of their drowsy grave and move again, having shed their old skin, with fresh nimbleness. Lend me your cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both, give my regards to the princes in our camp. Wish them good morning from me, and then ask them all to come to my pavilion.
KING HENRY V. No, my good knight. Go with my brothers to my lords of England. I and my own heart must debate for a while, and then I want no other company.
[Exeunt all but King.]
KING HENRY V. God reward you, old heart! You speak cheerfully.
[Enter Pistol.]
KING HENRY V. A friend.
KING HENRY V. I am a gentleman serving in a company.
KING HENRY V. Yes, I do. What are you?
KING HENRY V. Then you are better than the King.
KING HENRY V. Harry le Roy.
KING HENRY V. No, I am a Welshman.
KING HENRY V. Yes.
KING HENRY V. Don't wear your dagger in your cap that day, in case he knocks that about your head instead.
KING HENRY V. And his kinsman too.
KING HENRY V. I thank you. God be with you!
[Exit.]
KING HENRY V. It suits your fierceness well.
[Enter Fluellen and Gower.]
[Exeunt Gower and Fluellen.]
KING HENRY V. Though it seems a little old-fashioned, there is much care and valour in this Welshman.
[Enter three soldiers, John Bates, Alexander Court and Michael Williams.]
KING HENRY V. A friend.
KING HENRY V. Under Sir Thomas Erpingham.
KING HENRY V. He thinks we are like men wrecked on a sandbank, who expect to be washed off by the next tide.

KING HENRY V. No, and it isn't right that he should. Though I say it only to you, I think the King is just a man like me. The violet smells to him as it does to me. The sky looks to him as it does to me. All his senses have only human limits. Set aside his ceremonies, and in his nakedness he appears as only a man. His feelings are set higher than ours, but when they stoop, they stoop on the same wing. So when he sees reason for fear as we do, his fears are, without doubt, of the same flavour as ours. Still, it makes sense that no man should let him see any sign of fear, in case showing it discourages his army.
KING HENRY V. On my word, I will say what I truly think of the King: I think he would not wish himself anywhere but where he is.

KING HENRY V. I dare say you don't love him so badly as to wish him here alone, however you say it to test other men's minds. For my part, I think I could not die anywhere so contented as in the King's company, as long as his cause is just and his quarrel honourable.

KING HENRY V. So, by your rule, if a son is sent by his father on a trading voyage and dies sinfully at sea, the blame for his wickedness should fall on the father who sent him. Or if a servant, carrying a sum of money on his master's orders, is attacked by robbers and dies with many sins unforgiven, you could call the master's business the author of the servant's damnation. But this is not so. The King is not bound to answer for the particular endings of his soldiers, any more than the father for his son or the master for his servant. They do not intend their death when they intend their service. Besides, no king, however spotless his cause, can settle it by the judgment of swords with soldiers who are all spotless. Perhaps some carry the guilt of planned and plotted murder. Some have seduced virgins with the broken seals of perjury. Some are making the wars their shelter after they have wounded the gentle breast of Peace with pillage and robbery. Now if these men have cheated the law and outrun the punishment at home, though they can outstrip men, they have no wings to fly from God. War is his officer, war is his vengeance. So these men are punished, in the King's quarrel now, for breaking the King's laws before. Where they feared death, they escaped with their lives, and where they thought themselves safe, they perish. Then if they die unprepared, the King is no more guilty of their damnation than he was guilty before of the wickedness for which they are now visited. Every subject's duty belongs to the King, but every subject's soul is his own. So every soldier in the wars should do as every sick man in his bed: wash every speck out of his conscience. If he dies that way, death is a gain for him. If he does not die, the time was blessedly lost that bought such preparation. And in the man who escapes, it would be no sin to think that, because he made God so free an offer, God let him outlive that day to see His greatness and to teach others how to prepare.
KING HENRY V. I myself heard the King say he would not be ransomed.
KING HENRY V. If I live to see it, I will never trust his word again.
KING HENRY V. Your rebuke is somewhat too blunt. I would be angry with you if the time were right.
KING HENRY V. I accept it.
KING HENRY V. Give me some pledge of yours and I will wear it in my cap. Then, if you ever dare to acknowledge it, I will make it my quarrel.
KING HENRY V. There.
KING HENRY V. If I ever live to see it, I will challenge it.
KING HENRY V. Well, I will do it, even if I find you in the King's company.

KING HENRY V. Indeed, the French may bet twenty French crowns to one that they will beat us, because they carry them on their shoulders. But it is no English treason to cut French crowns, and tomorrow the King himself will be a clipper.
[Exeunt soldiers.]
[Enter Erpingham.]
KING HENRY V. Good old knight, gather them all together at my tent. I'll be there before you.
[Exit.]

KING HENRY V. Oh God of battles! Steel my soldiers' hearts. Do not fill them with fear. Take from them now the sense of counting, if the numbers against them tear their hearts from them. Not today, O Lord, oh, not today, do not think of the fault my father made in getting the crown! I have buried Richard's body again, and I have shed more contrite tears on it than the drops of blood that were forced from it. I have five hundred poor people on yearly pay, who twice a day hold up their withered hands toward heaven to ask pardon for that blood. I have built two chantries, where sad and solemn priests still sing for Richard's soul. I will do more. Though all I can do is worth nothing, since my penitence comes after everything, begging pardon.
[Enter Gloucester.]
KING HENRY V. My brother Gloucester's voice? Yes. I know your errand. I will go with you. The day, my friends, and everything else is waiting for me.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter the Dauphin, Orleans, Rambures and others.]
[Enter Constable.]
[Enter a Messenger.]
[Enter Grandpré.]
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Gloucester, Bedford, Exeter, Erpingham, with all his host: Salisbury and Westmorland.]
[Exit Salisbury.]
[Enter the King.]

KING HENRY V. Who is it that wishes that? My cousin Westmorland? No, my fair cousin. If we are marked out to die, we are enough to cause our country a loss. And if we are to live, the fewer men there are, the greater share of honour each has. By God's will, I beg you, wish for not one man more. By Jove, I am not greedy for gold, and I don't care who eats at my expense. It doesn't grieve me if men wear my clothes. Such outward things have no place in my desires. But if it is a sin to covet honour, I am the most offending soul alive. No, truly, my cousin, don't wish for a single man from England. By God's peace, I would not lose as much honour as one more man would, I think, take from my share, not for the best hope I have. Oh, don't wish for one more! Rather, Westmorland, proclaim through my army that any man who has no stomach for this fight may leave. His passport will be made out, and money for the journey put into his purse. We would not want to die in the company of a man who is afraid to die with us. This day is called the feast of Crispian. The man who outlives this day and comes safe home will stand on tiptoe when it is named and rouse himself at the name of Crispian. The man who lives through this day and sees old age will feast his neighbours every year on the eve and say, "Tomorrow is Saint Crispian." Then he will roll up his sleeve and show his scars and say, "I got these wounds on Crispian's day." Old men forget. Yet even if all else is forgotten, he will remember, with additions, what feats he did that day. Then our names, as familiar in his mouth as household words, Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter, Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester, will be freshly remembered in their flowing cups. The good man will teach this story to his son. And from this day to the end of the world, Crispin Crispian will never go by without our being remembered in it: we few, we happy few, we band of brothers. For the man who sheds his blood with me today will be my brother. However vile he is, this day will make him a gentleman. And gentlemen in England, now in bed, will think themselves cursed that they were not here, and will hold their manhood cheap whenever anyone speaks who fought with us upon Saint Crispin's day.
[Enter Salisbury.]
KING HENRY V. Everything is ready, if our minds are too.
KING HENRY V. You don't wish for more help from England, cousin?
KING HENRY V. Why, now you have unwished five thousand men, which pleases me better than wishing us one more. You know your places. God be with you all!
[Tucket. Enter Montjoy.]
KING HENRY V. Who has sent you now?

KING HENRY V. Please carry my former answer back. Tell them to win me first and then sell my bones. Good God! Why should they mock poor fellows like this? The man who once sold the lion's skin while the beast was alive was killed in hunting him. Many of our bodies will no doubt find graves in our homeland, and on those graves, I trust, a record of this day's work will live on in brass. And those who leave their valiant bones in France, dying like men, will be famous, even if they are buried in your dunghills. There the sun will greet them and draw their honours steaming up to heaven, leaving their earthly parts to choke your country, and the smell of them will breed a plague in France. Mark then the overflowing valour of our English, who, even dead, like a bullet that grazes, break out into a second course of mischief, killing as they fall back into death. Let me speak proudly. Tell the Constable we are only warriors for the working day. Our gaiety and our gilt are all smeared with rainy marching in the painful field. There is not a plume of feather in our army (good proof, I hope, that we will not fly), and time has worn us into shabbiness. But by the mass, our hearts are in good trim. And my poor soldiers tell me that before night they will be in fresher robes, or they will pull the gay new coats over the French soldiers' heads and turn them out of service. If they do this, as, if God pleases, they shall, then my ransom will soon be raised. Herald, save your trouble. Come no more for ransom, gentle herald. They shall have none, I swear, but these my joints. If they get those, as I will leave them to them, they will gain little, tell the Constable.
[Exit.]
KING HENRY V. I fear you will come again once more for ransom.
[Enter York.]
KING HENRY V. Take it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march on. And as it pleases you, God, arrange the day!
[Exeunt.]
[Alarum. Excursions. Enter Pistol, French Soldier and Boy.]
[Exeunt Pistol and French Soldier.]
[Exit.]
[Enter Constable, Orleans, Bourbon, Dauphin and Rambures.]
[A short alarum.]
[Exeunt.]
[Alarum. Enter King Henry and his train, with prisoners.]
KING HENRY V. We have done well, my thrice-valiant countrymen. But we are not finished yet, because the French still hold the field.
KING HENRY V. Is he alive, good uncle? Three times within this hour I saw him go down, and three times get up again and fight. He was covered in blood from helmet to spur.
KING HENRY V. I don't blame you. Hearing this, I have to strike a bargain with my misty eyes, or they will spill over too.
[Alarum.]
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Fluellen and Gower.]
[Alarum. Enter King Henry and forces; Warwick, Gloucester, Exeter with prisoners. Flourish.]

KING HENRY V. I have not been angry once since I came to France until this moment. Take a trumpet, herald, and ride to the horsemen on that hill over there. If they will fight us, tell them to come down, or else leave the field, because they offend our sight. If they will do neither, we will come to them and make them scatter as fast as stones shot from the old Assyrian slings. Besides, we'll cut the throats of the prisoners we hold, and not one of the men we take will taste our mercy. Go and tell them so.
[Enter Montjoy.]
KING HENRY V. How now! What does this mean, herald? Don't you know I have already put up these bones of mine as my ransom? Do you come again for ransom?
KING HENRY V. I tell you truly, herald, I don't know whether the day is ours or not. Many of your horsemen are still looking on and galloping over the field.
KING HENRY V. Praised be God, and not our strength, for it! What is that castle called that stands close by?
KING HENRY V. Then let us call this the field of Agincourt, fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.
KING HENRY V. They did, Fluellen.
KING HENRY V. I wear it as a memorable honor, for I am Welsh, you know, good countryman.
KING HENRY V. Thanks, my good countryman.
KING HENRY V. God keep me so!
[Enter Williams.]
[Exeunt Heralds with Montjoy.]
KING HENRY V. Soldier, why do you wear that glove in your cap?
KING HENRY V. An Englishman?
KING HENRY V. What do you think, Captain Fluellen? Is it right that this soldier keep his oath?
KING HENRY V. It may be that his enemy is a gentleman of high rank, well above the soldier's degree, and too high to answer him.
KING HENRY V. Then keep your vow, sirrah, when you meet the fellow.
KING HENRY V. Whom do you serve under?
KING HENRY V. Call him here to me, soldier.
[Exit.]

KING HENRY V. Here, Fluellen, wear this token for me and stick it in your cap. When Alençon and I were down together, I pulled this glove from his helmet. If any man challenges it, he is a friend to Alençon and an enemy to my person. If you meet any such man, arrest him, if you love me.
KING HENRY V. Do you know Gower?
KING HENRY V. Please go and look for him, and bring him to my tent.
[Exit.]

KING HENRY V. My Lord of Warwick, and my brother Gloucester, follow close at Fluellen's heels. The glove I gave him as a token may perhaps earn him a box on the ear. It is the soldier's. By our bargain I should be wearing it myself. Follow, good cousin Warwick. I judge from his blunt bearing that the soldier will keep his word and strike him. Some sudden mischief may come of it, because I know Fluellen is valiant and, once touched by anger, as hot as gunpowder, and he will quickly return an injury. Follow, and see that no harm comes between them. You come with me, uncle of Exeter.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Gower and Williams.]
[Enter Fluellen.]
[Strikes him.]
[Enter Warwick and Gloucester.]
[Enter King Henry and Exeter.]
KING HENRY V. What's this? What's the matter?
KING HENRY V. Give me your glove, soldier. Look, here is the other of the pair. It was I, indeed, whom you promised to strike, and you have given me the bitterest words.
KING HENRY V. How can you make me amends?
KING HENRY V. It was myself you abused.

KING HENRY V. Here, uncle Exeter, fill this glove with crowns and give it to this fellow. Keep it, fellow, and wear it as an honor in your cap until I challenge it. Give him his crowns. And, Captain, you must be friends with him.
[Enter an English Herald.]
KING HENRY V. Now, herald, have the dead been counted?
KING HENRY V. What prisoners of good rank have been taken, uncle?

KING HENRY V. This list tells me that ten thousand French lie slain in the field. Among them, princes and nobles who bear banners lie dead to the number of one hundred twenty-six. Added to these are eight thousand four hundred knights, esquires and gallant gentlemen, of whom five hundred were only made knights yesterday. So among the ten thousand they have lost, there are only sixteen hundred hired common soldiers. The rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires and gentlemen of blood and rank. Here are the names of those nobles of theirs who lie dead: Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; Jacques of Chatillon, Admiral of France; the master of the Crossbows, Lord Rambures; the Great Master of France, the brave Sir Guichard Dauphin; John, Duke of Alençon; Anthony, Duke of Brabant; the brother of the Duke of Burgundy; and Edward, Duke of Bar. Of lusty earls, Grandpré and Roussi, Fauconbridge and Foix, Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale. Here was a royal fellowship of death! Where is the number of our English dead?
[Herald gives him another paper.]
KING HENRY V. Come, let's go in procession to the village. And let it be proclaimed on pain of death throughout our army that no one is to boast of this or take from God the praise that is His alone.
KING HENRY V. Yes, Captain, but with this acknowledgment: that God fought for us.

KING HENRY V. Let us perform all the holy rites. Let _Non nobis_ and _Te Deum_ be sung, and let the dead be buried in the earth with charity. Then on to Calais, and then to England, where never from France arrived happier men.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Chorus.]
[Exit.]
[Enter Fluellen and Gower.]
[Enter Pistol.]
[Exit.]
[Exit.]
[Exit.]

[Enter at one door, King Henry, Exeter, Bedford, Warwick, Gloucester, Westmorland, Clarence, Huntingdon and other Lords. At another, Queen Isabel, the French King, the Princess Katherine, Alice, and other Ladies; the Duke of Burgundy and other French.]

KING HENRY V. Peace to this meeting, the reason we are all here! To our brother of France and our sister, I wish health and a good day. To our most fair and princely cousin Katharine, I wish joy and every good thing. And you, Duke of Burgundy, who are part of this royal family and who arranged this great gathering, I greet you too. And to the French princes and peers, I wish health to you all!
KING HENRY V. We have come here to say amen to that.

KING HENRY V. Duke of Burgundy, if you want the peace, and its absence is what lets the faults you described grow, then you must buy it. You must agree fully to all our just demands. You have their terms and details, set down briefly, in your hands.
KING HENRY V. Well, then, the peace you urged so strongly depends on his answer.

KING HENRY V. We will, brother. Go, uncle Exeter, and brother Clarence, and you, brother Gloucester. Warwick and Huntingdon, go with the King. Take full power with you to confirm, add to or change anything, in or out of our demands, as your wisdom sees best for our dignity. We will sign whatever you agree. Fair sister, will you go with the princes, or stay here with us?
KING HENRY V. But leave our cousin Katharine here with us. She is our main demand, and she is listed in the first rank of our articles.
[Exeunt all except Henry, Katherine and Alice.]
KING HENRY V. Fair Katharine, most fair, will you be kind enough to teach a soldier the words that will reach a lady's ear and plead his love to her gentle heart?
KATHERINE. Your Majesty will mock me. I cannot speak your England.
KING HENRY V. Oh fair Katharine, if you love me sincerely with your French heart, I will gladly hear you admit it in halting speech with your English tongue. Do you like me, Kate?
KATHERINE. _Pardonnez-moi_ — forgive me — I cannot tell what "like me" is.
KING HENRY V. An angel is like you, Kate, and you are like an angel.
KATHERINE. _Que dit-il? Que je suis semblable à les anges?_ — What does he say? That I am like the angels?
KING HENRY V. I did say so, dear Katharine, and I am not ashamed to stand by it.
KATHERINE. _O bon Dieu! les langues des hommes sont pleines de tromperies._ — Oh good God! The tongues of men are full of deceits.
KING HENRY V. What does she say, fair one? That the tongues of men are full of deceits?

KING HENRY V. The Princess is the better Englishwoman. In faith, Kate, my wooing suits your understanding. I am glad you can't speak better English. If you could, you would find me such a plain king that you would think I had sold my farm to buy my crown. I don't know how to dress up love. I can only say straight out, "I love you." If you press me further than that, to say "Do you, truly?", my suit is finished. Give me your answer, in faith, do. Then we clap hands and the bargain is struck. What do you say, lady?
KATHERINE. _Sauf votre honneur_ — saving your honor — I understand well.

KING HENRY V. Why, Kate, if you made me write verses or dance for your sake, you would ruin me. For the one I have neither words nor meter, and for the other I have no skill in step, though I have a fair amount of strength in step. If I could win a lady at leap-frog, or by vaulting into my saddle with my armor on my back, I would, if boasting may be pardoned, soon leap into a wife. Or if I could fight with fists for my love, or make my horse prance for her favor, I could lay on like a butcher and stick in the saddle like a monkey, never thrown. But before God, Kate, I can't look lovesick, or gasp out fine speeches, and I have no skill at making protestations. I only have plain oaths, which I never use until I'm pushed, and never break however hard I'm pushed. If you can love a fellow of this kind, Kate, whose face is not worth the sunburn, and who never looks in his mirror for love of anything he sees there, then let your eye be your cook. I speak to you as a plain soldier. If you can love me for this, take me. If not, to say I'd die of it would be true, but die for your love? By the Lord, no. Yet I do love you. And as long as you live, dear Kate, take a man of plain, unminted constancy. He must treat you rightly, because he has no gift for wooing elsewhere. These fellows with endless tongues, who can rhyme their way into ladies' favor, always reason their way out again. What! A speaker is only a prater. A rhyme is only a ballad. A good leg will fail. A straight back will stoop. A black beard will turn white. A curly head will go bald. A fair face will wither. A full eye will sink hollow. But a good heart, Kate, is the sun and the moon. Or rather the sun and not the moon, for it shines bright and never changes, but keeps its course faithfully. If you want such a man, take me. Take me, and you take a soldier. Take a soldier, and you take a king. So what do you say to my love? Speak, my fair one, and speak kindly, I beg you.
KATHERINE. Is it possible that I should love the enemy of France?

KING HENRY V. No, it is not possible that you should love the enemy of France, Kate. But in loving me you would love the friend of France. I love France so much that I will not give up a single village of it. I will have it all mine. And Kate, when France is mine and I am yours, then France is yours and you are mine.
KATHERINE. I cannot tell what that is.

KING HENRY V. No, Kate? I will tell you in French. I am sure it will cling to my tongue like a newly married wife around her husband's neck, hard to shake off. _Je quand sur le possession de France, et quand vous avez le possession de moi_ — when I have France, and when you have me — wait, let me see, what comes next? Saint Denis help me! — _donc votre est France, et vous êtes mienne_ — then France is yours and you are mine. It is as easy for me, Kate, to conquer the kingdom as to speak that much more French. I will never move you in French, unless it is to make you laugh at me.
KATHERINE. _Sauf votre honneur, le français que vous parlez, il est meilleur que l'anglais lequel je parle._ — Saving your honor, the French that you speak is better than the English that I speak.

KING HENRY V. No, faith, it is not, Kate. But my speaking your tongue and your speaking mine, both truly false, must be admitted to be much the same. But Kate, do you understand this much English: can you love me?
KATHERINE. I cannot tell.

KING HENRY V. Can any of your neighbors tell, Kate? I'll ask them. Come, I know you love me. Tonight, when you go into your private room, you will question this gentlewoman about me. And I know, Kate, that to her you will run down the very qualities in me that you love in your heart. But, good Kate, mock me mercifully, all the more, gentle princess, because I love you cruelly. If you are ever mine, Kate, as a saving faith inside me says you will be, I will have won you in a scramble, so you must prove a good breeder of soldiers. Shall you and I, between Saint Denis and Saint George, not make a boy, half French and half English, who will go to Constantinople and take the Turk by the beard? Shall we not? What do you say, my fair flower-de-luce?
KATHERINE. I do not know that.

KING HENRY V. No, that is for later to know, but for now to promise. Just promise now, Kate, that you will do your best, for your French part, toward such a boy. For my English half, take the word of a king and a bachelor. How do you answer, _la plus belle Katherine du monde, mon très cher et divin déesse?_ — the most beautiful Katherine in the world, my most dear and divine goddess?
KATHERINE. Your Majesty has _fausse_ — false — French enough to deceive the most _sage demoiselle_ — wise young lady — that is _en France_ — in France.

KING HENRY V. Now, curse my false French! By my honor, in true English, I love you, Kate. By that same honor I dare not swear that you love me. Yet my blood begins to flatter me that you do, in spite of my poor, unsoftening face. Now, curse my father's ambition! He was thinking of civil wars when he fathered me. So I was made with a stubborn outside and an iron look, and when I come to woo ladies I frighten them. But in faith, Kate, the older I get, the better I will look. My comfort is that old age, that bad keeper of beauty, can do no more damage to my face. You have me, if you have me, at my worst. And you will wear me, if you wear me, better and better. So tell me, most fair Katharine, will you have me? Put off your maidenly blushes. Declare the thoughts of your heart with the look of an empress. Take me by the hand and say, "Harry of England, I am yours." The moment you bless my ear with those words, I will tell you aloud: England is yours, Ireland is yours, France is yours, and Henry Plantagenet is yours. He, though I say it to his face, if he is not the equal of the best king, you will find the best king of good fellows. Come, give me your answer in broken music, for your voice is music and your English is broken. So, queen of all, Katharine, break your mind to me in broken English. Will you have me?
KATHERINE. That is as it shall please _le roi mon père_ — the king my father.
KING HENRY V. Why, it will please him well, Kate. It shall please him, Kate.
KATHERINE. Then it shall also content me.
KING HENRY V. On that I kiss your hand and call you my queen.

KATHERINE. _Laissez, mon seigneur, laissez, laissez!_ — Stop, my lord, stop, stop! — _Ma foi, je ne veux point que vous abaissiez votre grandeur en baisant la main d'une—Notre Seigneur!—indigne serviteur._ — Truly, I do not want you to lower your greatness by kissing the hand of an — Our Lord! — unworthy servant. — _Excusez-moi, je vous supplie, mon très-puissant seigneur._ — Excuse me, I beg you, my most powerful lord.
KING HENRY V. Then I will kiss your lips, Kate.

KATHERINE. _Les dames et demoiselles pour être baisées devant leurs noces, il n'est pas la coutume de France._ — For ladies and young ladies to be kissed before their wedding is not the custom of France.
KING HENRY V. Madam my interpreter, what does she say?
KING HENRY V. To kiss.
KING HENRY V. Is she saying it is not the fashion for maids in France to kiss before they are married?

KING HENRY V. Oh Kate, nice customs bow to great kings. Dear Kate, you and I cannot be confined within the weak fence of one country's fashion. We are the makers of manners, Kate. The freedom that comes with our rank shuts the mouth of every fault-finder, as I will shut yours, for upholding your country's fussy fashion by denying me a kiss. So, patiently and yielding. [_Kissing her._] You have witchcraft in your lips, Kate. There is more eloquence in one sugar touch of them than in the tongues of the whole French council. They would persuade Harry of England sooner than a general petition from monarchs. Here comes your father.
[Enter the French Power and the English Lords.]
KING HENRY V. I would like her to learn, my fair cousin, how perfectly I love her. And that is good English.

KING HENRY V. Our tongue is rough, cousin, and my nature is not smooth. I have neither the voice nor the heart of flattery in me. So I cannot conjure up the spirit of love in her so that he appears in his true shape.
KING HENRY V. Yet maidens do shut their eyes and yield, since love is blind and forces them.
KING HENRY V. Then, my good lord, teach your cousin to consent with her eyes shut.
KING HENRY V. This lesson ties me to waiting for time and a hot summer. So I will catch the fly, your cousin, at the end of the season, and she must be blind too.
KING HENRY V. So it is. And some of you may thank love for my blindness, since I cannot see many a fair French city because of one fair French maid who stands in my way.
KING HENRY V. Shall Kate be my wife?
KING HENRY V. I am content, as long as the maiden cities you speak of wait on her. Then the maid who stood in the way of my wish will show me the way to my will.
KING HENRY V. Is that so, my lords of England?
KING HENRY V. Then I ask you, in love and dear alliance, to let that one article rank with the rest. And on that, give me your daughter.
KING HENRY V. Now, welcome, Kate. And all of you, bear me witness that here I kiss her as my sovereign queen.
[Flourish.]

KING HENRY V. Let us prepare for our marriage. On that day, my Lord of Burgundy, we will take your oath and the oath of all the peers, as security for our alliances. Then I shall swear to Kate, and you to me. And may our oaths be well kept and prosperous!
[Sennet. Exeunt.]
[Enter Chorus.]
[Exit.]
